summary:
Oakland to the Moon is a single-player, 16-bit space mission simulation game that transforms complex aerospace engineering concepts into an interactive educational experience. Inspired by classic SNES games, it follows Commander Kai, an astronaut from Oakland, California, on a journey from his hometown to space.
Players take on the role of mission designers, making critical decisions about spacecraft construction, propulsion, fuel, power, life support, scientific instruments, budgets, and mission planning. Every decision has consequences, requiring players to balance competing engineering constraints to complete lunar exploration or International Space Station missions.
Developed for the NASA Space Apps Challenge, our game addresses the difficulty of understanding how individual spacecraft systems work together. By combining NASA-inspired engineering models, interactive calculations, realistic mission trade-offs, and educational feedback, players learn through experimentation rather than theory alone.
Our goal is to make space mission engineering accessible, engaging, and inspiring, especially for students and aspiring engineers who may never have had the opportunity to explore aerospace design firsthand.
details:
Oakland to the Moon — Project Details

What does our project do?

Oakland to the Moon is an interactive, browser-based educational game that allows players to experience the process of designing, launching, and managing space missions.

The game follows Commander Kai, a fictional astronaut from Oakland, California, selected to participate in an ambitious lunar exploration program. Players begin with a story-driven introduction set in Oakland before taking responsibility for the engineering decisions needed to make the mission successful.

The game includes two mission experiences: a crewed lunar mission involving launch, lunar transit, landing, surface exploration, and return to Earth; and an International Space Station mission involving orbital operations, docking, and a spacewalk.

How does it work?

Players configure their spacecraft by selecting components and mission parameters while balancing engineering requirements.

The simulation evaluates interconnected resources and constraints, including:

  • Mass and propulsion: Spacecraft weight, rocket performance, propellant requirements, and delta-v.
  • Electrical systems: Power generation, battery reserves, and energy consumption.
  • Crew survival: Oxygen, water, life support, and mission duration.
  • Communications and science: Data generation, onboard storage, communication capabilities, and scientific objectives.
  • Mission planning: Launch vehicle selection, mission architecture, orbital decisions, budgets, and operational risks.

The spacecraft builder provides immediate feedback showing how engineering decisions affect mission feasibility.

Players can also use an interactive calculation desk to explore engineering relationships, review design warnings, and respond to emergencies inspired by real spaceflight events.

After completing or failing a mission, players receive a performance report evaluating their scientific accomplishments, engineering decisions, resource efficiency, and overall mission success.

This allows players to learn from mistakes, redesign their spacecraft, and experiment with alternative approaches.

What benefits does the project provide?

Space mission design is typically taught through theoretical exercises or advanced engineering software. These approaches can be difficult for beginners to understand because they often require significant technical knowledge.

Oakland to the Moon makes these concepts approachable by transforming engineering decisions into interactive gameplay.

Instead of simply reading about propulsion, players experience how insufficient fuel affects mission feasibility. Rather than memorizing electrical systems concepts, they see how power generation and battery reserves influence spacecraft operations.

The game also demonstrates that there is rarely one perfect spacecraft design. Different engineering configurations can achieve similar mission objectives through different trade-offs.

What is the intended impact?

Our goal is to inspire greater interest in aerospace engineering, computer science, and STEM education by making space exploration accessible to a broader audience.

The Oakland setting is especially meaningful to our project. By featuring an astronaut from Oakland, California, we wanted to communicate that a career in science and space exploration can begin in any community.

We hope the game encourages students to see engineering as something they can actively explore, rather than an intimidating subject reserved for specialists.

The game is accessible directly through a web browser, allowing students, educators, and space enthusiasts to experiment with mission design without purchasing specialized software.

What tools and technologies did we use?

We developed Oakland to the Moon using the following technologies:

  • TypeScript: Implements spacecraft systems, engineering calculations, mission progression, and gameplay logic.
  • Phaser 3: Provides the 2D game engine for scenes, character movement, interactive menus, animations, and visual effects.
  • Vite: Handles local development and production builds.
  • Procedural pixel-art generation: Creates original 16-bit-style environments, spacecraft components, characters, and interface artwork through code.
  • Web Audio API: Generates original retro-inspired sound effects and music.
  • Vitest: Tests individual engineering calculations and simulation behavior.
  • Playwright: Automates browser testing, including complete mission playthroughs.
  • Git and GitHub: Support version control, collaboration, and project management.
  • GitHub Actions and GitHub Pages: Automate testing, building, and hosting the browser-based game.
  • Claude Code and AI-assisted development tools: Accelerated programming, code review, debugging, asset generation, and development iteration under team direction.

The engineering model incorporates simplified aerospace relationships, including the Tsiolkovsky rocket equation, with reference to NASA mission-design resources and real spacecraft specifications. Where necessary, physical processes are simplified to maintain accessibility and engaging gameplay.

What makes our project creative?

The most distinctive aspect of Oakland to the Moon is its combination of retro video game storytelling with interactive aerospace systems engineering.

Rather than creating a conventional educational dashboard, we developed an experience inspired by classic 16-bit video games, featuring original pixel-art environments, animated spacecraft, character dialogue, mission-control interfaces, and cinematic sequences.

The game connects its fictional Oakland-based story with genuine engineering challenges.

The modular spacecraft builder visually reflects players' component selections, while the simulation demonstrates the resulting engineering consequences.

Players are not simply rewarded for selecting the most expensive equipment. They must consider trade-offs between scientific value, mass, fuel, electrical power, budget, and mission reliability.

Our inclusion of lunar exploration and International Space Station scenarios also allows players to experience different mission objectives and operational constraints within the same educational framework.

What factors did our team consider?

Throughout development, we prioritized five principles:

  1. Scientific credibility: Use meaningful engineering relationships while clearly documenting simplified models and fictional gameplay values.
  2. Accessibility: Make aerospace concepts understandable to students and beginners without requiring advanced mathematical knowledge.
  3. Educational value: Explain why designs succeed or fail and encourage learning through experimentation.
  4. Engaging presentation: Use a distinctive Oakland-inspired narrative and cohesive SNES-style graphics to make engineering more approachable.
  5. Technical reliability: Maintain separation between rendering and simulation logic, use automated testing, and deploy the game as an accessible browser application.

Our final implementation was validated through 195 passing unit tests and seven passing automated browser tests, including complete lunar and International Space Station mission playthroughs.

Conclusion

Oakland to the Moon demonstrates that complex space mission engineering can be transformed into an engaging and accessible learning experience.

By combining scientific modeling, resource management, interactive decision-making, original retro artwork, and storytelling rooted in Oakland, our project encourages players to think like aerospace engineers while discovering that space exploration is within reach of the next generation.
